## Rule based detection {.smaller}
How would you identify where the cells are in this image?

![](img/ml_raw_image.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="25%" left="0%" width="49%"}

![](img/ml_brightness_threshold.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="25%" right="0%" width="49%"}

## Rule based detection {.smaller}

Adding a second measurement, like cell size, lets you separate cells from noise

![](img/ml_size_threshold_scatter.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="32%" left="4%" width="46%"}

![](img/ml_size_threshold_image.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="32%" right="4%" width="46%"}


## Fitting the boundary from data {.smaller}

We can fit a boundary from the data itself, rather than picking a threshold by eye

![](img/ml_linear_combo.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="29%" left="16%" width="70%"}

## Logistic regression {.smaller}

Collapse both measurements into a single score, then fit a sigmoid function

score  =  w₁ · width  +  w₂ · brightness  +  b  =  0.29 · width  +  0.02 · brightness  − 7.6

![](img/ml_logistic_regression.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="17%" left="12%" width="76%"}

::: {.fragment .absolute bottom="4%" left="12%" style="width: 76%;"}
17 px wide, brightness 183 → score **+1.0** → cell

3 px wide, brightness 109 → score **−4.5** → not a cell
:::

## Real data is complex! {.smaller}

No straight boundary can separate these two groups - wherever you put it, it cuts through the wrong points

![](img/ml_boundary_needs_more.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="6%" left="8%" width="84%"}

## Fitting complex relationships {.smaller}

Change the question from *"is this a cell?"* to *"is this exactly one cell?"*

![](img/ml_two_sigmoids.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="27%" left="17%" width="66%"}

## Fitting complex relationships {.smaller}

Nothing about the target is sigmoid shaped. Add enough single sigmoids, each with its own fitted weight, and the sum can take essentially any shape.

![](img/ml_many_sigmoids.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="6%" left="8%" width="84%"}

## How the weights are found {.smaller}

Relies on having a loss that estimates model performance

![](img/ml_training_loop.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="6%" left="8%" width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
Three things to say:

1. The **loss** is one number: how wrong the model is on the training data.
   Nothing else in training is being optimised.
2. A **step** measures the loss, works out which way each weight should move
   to lower it, and moves it a little. That is gradient descent; the "little"
   is the learning rate.
3. An **epoch** is one pass over the training set. Training is thousands of
   steps.

Worth naming the honest gap in the picture: real loss surfaces are in
millions of dimensions, not one, and they are not this smooth.
:::

# What is a neural net?

## A combination of units {background-color="black" .smaller}

![](img/fully_connected.png){.nostretch .absolute top="16%" left="20%" height="60%"}

::: {.absolute bottom="4%" left="6%" style="width: 88%; color: white;"}
::: {.fragment}
Every pixel feeds every unit in the first layer, and each unit is the same as the last few slides: a weight per input, a bias, a squash. The ten outputs are: [0, 1, 2, ..., 10]
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
784 inputs x ~100 units is already ~78,000 weights for a thumbnail.
:::

## Architecture: wiring the units {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Fully connected layers: every unit in one layer connects to every unit in the next
- Convolutional layers: each unit only connects to a small patch of the previous layer
- Transformer layers: every unit can read every other, but how much it reads each one is computed from the input itself
:::

::: {.fragment}
All of these are just different ways to wire up regression units.
:::

# Training and testing

## Train, validation, test split {.smaller}

Split the data once, three ways — and treat the test set as spent the moment you look at it.

![](img/ml_split_three_way.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="28%" left="8%" width="84%"}

::: {.fragment .absolute bottom="6%" left="8%" style="width: 84%;"}
Memorising practice answers != learning biology.
:::

::: {.notes}
The test set is the one thing here that cannot be undone. Look at it twice —
tweak anything after seeing it — and you no longer have a clean number to
report, because you have started fitting to it by hand.
:::

## Scoring a model {.smaller}

Every claim about performance is one number, computed by comparing predictions to labels on one split

::: {.incremental}
- **Accuracy** — fraction of calls that were right. Misleading when one class is rare: call everything "background" in a sparse image and you score 99%
- **Precision** — of the things you called cells, how many were cells? Low precision = false positives
- **Recall** — of the cells that were there, how many did you find? Low recall = false negatives
- **F1** — a combined metric, so a model can't win by being timid or trigger-happy
:::

::: {.fragment}
Precision and recall **trade off**: lower the detection threshold and recall goes up while precision goes down
:::

## Generalisation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- A model that generalises scores as well on unseen data as on training data
- **Underfitting**: too little capacity, or too little training — poor on both
- **Overfitting**: enough capacity to memorise the training set — good on train, poor on test
:::

::: {.fragment}
Test labels are human opinions too. 95% recall against one annotator's boundaries is not 95% against the biology.
:::

## Underfitting {.smaller}

Too little capacity to represent the relationship at all - so it is wrong on the training data as well as on unseen data.

![](img/ml_underfitting.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="8%" left="10%" width="80%"}

## Overfitting {.smaller}

Same loop as before, now scored on both splits after every epoch.

![](img/ml_overfitting_curves.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="28%" left="14%" width="72%"}

# From pixels to meaning

## Pixels don't scale {background-color="black" .smaller}

![](img/fully_connected.png){.nostretch .absolute top="16%" left="20%" height="60%"}

::: {.fragment .absolute bottom="4%" left="6%" style="width: 88%; color: white;"}
784 pixels for a thumbnail digit — a single tile of imaging data is millions. Almost all of it is empty background! The actual information is sparse
:::

::: {.notes}
Two separate objections, worth separating out loud:

1. Cost — wiring every pixel to every unit grows the weight count with the
   image, and the network has to learn "a cell is a cell" independently at
   every position.
2. Redundancy — neighbouring pixels are nearly identical, and most of a brain
   slice is background. Millions of numbers carrying very little.

The fix is to stop working in pixels and work in something denser.
:::

## The compression funnel {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**pixel space**

millions of numbers, mostly redundant
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**embedding space**

a few hundred numbers, in which like sits near like
:::
:::
:::

![](img/ml_embedding_funnel.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="8%" left="8%" width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
Like reducing a transcript to its themes — you lose the exact wording and gain
something more useful to work with.

The right-hand panel is the payoff, and it is worth naming: after the
squeeze, things of the same kind land near each other. That is what makes the
classifier's job easy, and it is exactly what transfers when someone else's
embedding space is reused on your data — the next slide.
:::

# Convolutional Neural Networks

## A window that slides {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The same small window of weights is applied everywhere in the image
- Where it matches, it writes a high value into a feature map
:::

![](img/convolution.gif){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="16%" left="34%" width="32%"}

::: {.notes}
Blue is the input, green is the feature map the window writes into; the
dashed border is padding so the edges get treated like everywhere else.
:::

## Increasingly abstract spotters {.smaller}

Early layers find edges; later layers combine them into shapes, then parts, then a name

![](img/increasing_complexity.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="4%" left="20%" width="60%"}

::: {.notes}
Figure from Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, *Deep Learning* (2016), fig 1.2.

This is the intuition for depth. Each layer's units look at what the previous
layer found, not at raw pixels — so "meaning" accumulates with depth: pixels,
edges, corners and contours, object parts, object identity.
:::

## Detection vs segmentation {background-color="black" .smaller}

![](img/ml_detect_vs_segment.png){.nostretch .absolute top="17%" left="8%" width="84%"}

::: {.absolute bottom="6%" left="8%" style="width: 84%; color: white;"}
:::: {.columns}
::::: {.column width="50%"}
:::::: {.fragment}
Detection — a point per cell
::::::
:::::
::::: {.column width="50%"}
:::::: {.fragment}
Segmentation — every pixel is a cell or background
::::::
:::::
::::
:::

# U-Net: built for segmentation

## The U shape {.smaller}

Zoom out for context, zoom back in to trace the exact outline.

![](img/ml_unet.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="10%" left="8%" width="84%"}

## Skip connections {.smaller}

Without them the decoder only has the blurry bottleneck to work from.

![](img/ml_unet_skip.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="10%" left="8%" width="84%"}

## Input -> precise mask {background-color="black" .smaller}

![](img/ml_mask_output.png){.nostretch .absolute top="24%" left="8%" width="84%"}

## Scoring a mask: IoU {.smaller}

Precision and recall need a rule for when a predicted cell *is* a labelled cell. For masks, that rule is overlap.

![](img/iou.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="24%" left="26%" width="48%"}

::: {.notes}
IoU — intersection over union — is 1 for a perfect match and 0 for no
overlap. Segmentation papers report things like "AP@0.5 IoU": count a cell as
found if its mask overlaps the label by at least 0.5, then compute
precision/recall on those calls.

So the metric has a knob in it. Tighten the threshold and the same model
scores worse. Whenever someone quotes a segmentation number, ask what
threshold it was at — and remember the labels underneath are still one
person's boundaries.
:::

# Vision Transformers

## Attention, in words {.smaller}

In "the animal didn't cross the street because **it** was too tired", what does "it" refer to?

![](img/attention_words.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="25%" left="32%" width="36%"}

::: {.notes}
Each colour is a different attention head, looking for a different kind of
relationship: one links "it" to "animal" (what it refers to), another to
"street" and "tired". Nothing here was hand-coded; the weights came out of
training.
:::

## Attention, in images {.smaller}

Same idea on pixels: the model decides for itself which parts of the image matter

![](img/attention.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="20%" left="38%" width="35%"}

::: {.notes}
Right column is the attention map — bright where the model is looking. It
finds the dog, the plane and the snake without ever being told where they
are, and without a sliding window.

Contrast with the CNN: a convolution always looks at a fixed local
neighbourhood. Attention can link two patches at opposite corners if the
image warrants it.
:::

## ViT: patches, like words {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The image is cut into fixed-size patches, and each patch is treated like a word
- The stack of patches goes through the same machinery to generate an embedding
- A simple network on top can use this embedding to predict the output
:::

![](img/vit_architecture.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="34%" left="26%" width="48%"}

::: {.notes}
Matters later because SAM's backbone is a ViT. One analogy, one slide, move
on — but do point at the "linear projection of flattened patches" box and
say that is the pixels-to-embedding step from earlier, done per patch.
:::

# From scratch vs fine-tuning

## Training from scratch {.smaller}

:::{.incremental}
- Complex model architectures take longer to train and need more data
- Large foundational models are trained on 100k - 1 billion images!
   - `cellfinder` was trained on 100k hand labelled cells
- Generating the data takes too long
:::

## Fine-tuning {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Starting from random weights doesn't always make sense!
- Sometimes you want to reuse the encoder/embeddings from other models
- Feed a small number (100s to 1000s) of your data to teach the model "your" data
:::

# Building your training set

## Test set leakage {.smaller}

Splitting images randomly isn't the same as splitting subjects randomly

::: {.incremental}
- If one animal contributes images to both the training set and the test set, the model can partly identify it: same tissue, same staining batch, same imaging session
- The test score then reflects memorisation of that subject, not real generalisation
- Fix: split by subject (or by acquisition session) first, then assign every image from that subject to train, validation, *or* test — never split across
:::

## Split the animals, not the images {.smaller}

![](img/ml_split_by_subject.png){.nostretch .absolute top="24%" left="10%" width="80%"}

## Statistical not causal {.smaller}

A model learns whatever correlates with the label, which may not necessarily be the biology!

::: {.incremental}
- Chest X-ray models trained to detect COVID-19 were found to rely on features *outside the lungs entirely* — image borders, laterality markers, patient positioning
- If every positive scan came from one hospital, the model can learn that hospital's scanner artefacts instead of the disease
:::

::: {.fragment}
The model is statistical, not causal. It will happily use a confound if the confound is easier to learn than the real biology.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: DeGrave, Janizek & Lee, "AI for radiographic COVID-19 detection
selects shortcuts over signal", Nature Machine Intelligence 2021.

Ask: what confound could sneak into a cell-detection dataset? Target answers:
imaging session, animal, microscope, time of day — same traps as test set
leakage, one level up.
:::

## Human-in-the-loop {.smaller}

Most fine-tuning data comes from correcting the model's own mistakes.

![](img/ml_human_loop.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="4%" left="22%" width="56%"}

# The tool landscape

## ilastik {.smaller}

Learning, without deep learning

::: {.incremental}
- You paint a few pixels of your target and a few of background
- A classical classifier (random forest) learns the boundary between them
- Interactive: you see the result and paint more where it's wrong
:::

## StarDist {.smaller}

A shape prior instead of free-form pixels

::: {.incremental}
- Predicts, for each pixel, the distances to the object boundary along fixed rays — a star-convex polygon
- Because every cell is one polygon, touching cells come out as separate objects rather than one merged blob
:::

![](img/ml_stardist_rays.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="9%" left="18%" width="64%"}

## Cellpose 2 {.smaller}

A U-Net that predicts flows, plus retraining in the loop

::: {.incremental}
- Instead of a mask, it predicts for each pixel a direction pointing towards its cell's centre; pixels that flow to the same point are one cell
- Generalist model trained on a large, deliberately varied collection of cell images
- Ships with human-in-the-loop retraining: correct a few cells, fine-tune, carry on
:::

![](img/ml_cellpose_flows.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="9%" left="18%" width="64%"}

## Segment Anything (SAM) {.smaller}

The foundation-model move: one model, fine-tuned

::: {.incremental}
- ViT backbone, trained on SA-1B: ~11 million natural images, ~1 billion masks — of which only ~10 million over ~300k images were drawn by hand; the rest the model generated and a filter kept
- Promptable: click a point or drag a box, get a mask — no retraining
- Knows "object", not "cell", out of the box it does poorly on microscopy images
:::

## Cellpose-SAM {.smaller}

Fine-tuning a foundation model onto cells

::: {.incremental}
- Takes SAM's pretrained ViT backbone and trains it on Cellpose's cellular datasets
- Deliberately trained against realistic degradations — blur, noise, anisotropy, channel order — so it holds up on data it hasn't seen
- Approaches human-to-human agreement on their test set
:::

::: {.notes}
Pachitariu, Rariden & Stringer, bioRxiv 2025. The annotator-agreement
framing is the honest way to read that headline number, and it closes the
loop with the second slide of the lecture.
:::

## cellfinder {.smaller}

Detection for large 3D imaging datasets

::: {.incremental}
- Classical filtering proposes candidate cells; a small CNN classifies each candidate as cell or artefact
- Detection, not segmentation: counts and coordinates not outlines
- Ships with a pretrained network, which can (should!) be fine-tuned
:::
